sec: Half-lives and CaSR mutation disorders · p876

items.q: Match half-lives — 1) PTH  2) Calcitriol  3) 25(OH)D3 … A) 6–8 hours  B) 2–3 weeks  C) 2–4 minutes
items.exp: PTH 2–4 min; calcitriol 6–8 hours; 25(OH)D3 2–3 weeks (used for blood level estimations). (Book p876)

items.q: The metabolite used for blood-level estimation of vitamin D (longest half-life) is:
items.exp: 25(OH)D3 (2–3 weeks) is used for blood level estimations. (Book p876)
Gain-of-function CaSR → Bartter type V, AD (all other Bartter types AR). (Book p876)

items.q: ‘Bartter syndrome type V is autosomal dominant, whereas all other Bartter types are autosomal recessive.’
opts: True, but type V is X-linked
items.exp: Type V AD; all other Bartter types AR. (Book p876)

items.q: In Bartter type V, excessive CaSR activation causes:
items.exp: Excessive CaSR activation → ↑↑↑ excretion → hypocalcaemia; all other Bartters show hypercalcaemia. (Book p876)

items.q: A LOSS-of-function CaSR mutation (seen in children, AD) produces:
items.exp: Loss-of-function → FHH, autosomal dominant, seen in children. (Book p876)

opts: Failure of CaSR activation → no excretion → complete reabsorption → hypocalciuria + hypercalcaemia
items.exp: Failure of CaSR activation → no excretion → complete reabsorption → hypocalciuria + hypercalcaemia. (Book p876)
